target: Mesopotamia (the Inter-River) is a plain in the Tigris and Euphrates river basin, extending northwest from the Persian Gulf to the Upper Euphrates. Today, it is largely part of Iraq. This extensive region is divided into two parts: Lower Mesopotamia, situated in the lower reaches of the Tigris and Euphrates, where the riverbeds converge (today they even merge into the single river, the Shatt al-Arab; in antiquity, they flowed into the gulf as separate channels), and Upper (Northern) Mesopotamia, where the Euphrates and Tigris are far apart. In antiquity, Lower Mesopotamia was called Sumer (in the broadest sense of the word) and was further divided into southern and northern parts. The south of Lower Mesopotamia was known as the Coastal Land, or Sumer "in the narrow sense of the word," while the north was initially called Ki-Uri and later Akkad (after the city of Akkad located there, the Mesopotamian capital at the end of the 3rd millennium BCE). Hence the name for Lower Mesopotamia as a whole, which became established in the late 3rd millennium BCE: "Sumer and Akkad." Still later, Lower Mesopotamia came to be called Babylonia, after its new main center, Babylon.

The history of ancient Mesopotamia spans several millennia and is traditionally divided in scholarship into a series of periods: prehistoric – the Ubaid period (6th–4th millennia BCE); the Uruk period (4th millennium BCE); the Jemdet Nasr period (late 4th–early 3rd millennia BCE); and historical – the Early Dynastic period with three sub-periods (30th–24th centuries BCE); the era of the first despotisms – the Akkadian and Ur III periods (24th–21st centuries BCE); the Old Babylonian–Old Assyrian period (20th–16th centuries BCE), the Middle Babylonian–Middle Assyrian period (16th/15th–12th/11th centuries BCE), and the Neo-Assyrian period (10th–7th centuries BCE) – the Neo-Babylonian period (12th–6th centuries BCE), with some discrepancies in the periodization of Babylonia and Assyria; finally, the Late Babylonian period (6th/5th century BCE – the turn of the eras), when Mesopotamia was part of foreign empires. Below, these periods are further subdivided into three major stages: prehistory (up to the beginning of the Early Dynastic period), early antiquity (from the Early Dynastic to the beginning of the Neo-Assyrian period, 3rd–2nd millennia BCE), and late antiquity (the Neo-Assyrian period and later, 1st millennium BCE).

Below, these periods are further subdivided into three major stages: prehistory (up to the beginning of the Early Dynastic period), early antiquity (from the Early Dynastic to the beginning of the Neo-Assyrian period, 3rd–2nd millennia BCE), and late antiquity (the Neo-Assyrian period and later, 1st millennium BCE).

target: Who were the bearers of the preceding, Ubaid culture? Many scholars believe they were also Sumerians. However, the change in ceramic styles, and especially in burial practices, is usually associated with the arrival of a new ethnic group. Furthermore, the Sumerian language contains loanwords from a more ancient language – these are terms related to crafts and some names (including the names of gods, such as Alalu, Kubaba, and Zababa). Such names were common among the people who lived north of Sumer, in a region called “Subir” or “Subar” (where Ubaid culture was also widespread). The Sumerians themselves believed that their history once began with two communities: one in “Eridu” (the city that the Sumerians considered their oldest settlement), and the other defined as Subarian. From this, it appears that the Ubaid culture belonged to a distinct pre-Sumerian people, and the aforementioned names and terms were derived from their language. The Sumerians only arrived here in the early 4th millennium BCE, mixed with the local population, and assimilated them. As a result, the Uruk period began in Lower Mesopotamia – the first period of Sumerian history – while to the north of it, tribes from the same pre-Sumerian ethnic area continued to exist. The Sumerians called their northern territory “Subar” and its inhabitants “the Subarian people.” Since the Sumerians retained some memory of the fact that their history in Mesopotamia began with a mingling with this same people, they portrayed this history as the product of a symbiosis between Sumerian Eridu and “Subar,” which represented the indigenous population.

target: In the late 4th millennium BCE, or shortly thereafter, a distinct branch of Semites – the eastern Semites, later termed “Akkadians” in scholarship – migrated to Mesopotamia from northern Arabia. Part of the eastern Semites settled in the northern half of the territory occupied by the Sumerians (as a result of which this region received a special Sumerian name, Ki-Uri), while the other part settled outside it, in the Middle Tigris region. The first group of eastern Semites, who intermingled with the Sumerians and eventually assimilated them all, gave rise to the Babylonian people, and the second group gave rise to the Assyrian people. The Babylonian and Assyrian languages are different dialects of the eastern Semitic (Akkadian) language, which became distinct from each other around the turn of the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE.

target: Following the Uruk period, archaeologists distinguish the Jemdet Nasr period (late 4th millennium BCE), named after another settlement site where a later archive was discovered, demonstrating further development of pictographic writing. The Uruk and Jemdet Nasr periods are sometimes combined into a “Proto-cuneiform period.” With the transition from pictography to a fully developed syllabic writing system and a series of other changes in material culture and social life, the subsequent Early Dynastic period in Mesopotamian history begins (late 4th millennium – 24th century BCE). This was the period of the existence of Sumerian city-states. It was during the Early Dynastic period that Eastern Semitic peoples – the Akkadians – living in symbiosis with the Sumerians, became the second component of the population of Lower Mesopotamia. Archaeologically, the Early Dynastic period is divided into three stages (early 3rd millennium, the second quarter and mid-third quarter of the 3rd millennium BCE). The boundary between the first and second of these stages is marked by a major flood, which remained in the memory of the Mesopotamians – the so-called “Great Flood” (c. 2950 BCE).

target: In the late 24th century BCE, Lower Mesopotamia was, for the first time, united into a centralized empire with the absolute power of a king. This empire was established by the Akkad dynasty (24th–22nd centuries BCE) and later restored by the so-called Third Dynasty of Ur (late 21st–20th centuries BCE). The power of Ur was shattered around 2003 BCE by the invasion of new Semitic nomadic groups – the Amorites. The First Dynasty of Isin (2017–1794 BCE) attempted to continue the statehood, but a large part of the country soon fell outside of its control, and Mesopotamia fragmented into numerous kingdoms. The reigns of the “imperial” dynasties of Akkad and Ur are collectively known as the period of the first centralized despotisms in Mesopotamia (c. 2316–2003 BCE).

target: The unification of Mesopotamia was not achieved until the mid-18th century BCE, when the famous Babylonian king Hammurabi, himself from the Amorite dynasty, accomplished it. The period of this dynasty’s rule in Babylon is considered a distinct Old Babylonian period in Mesopotamian history (1895–1595 BCE). After this, power over Babylonia passed to a dynasty from the Kassite people, a group of highlanders, and their rule forms the subsequent Middle Babylonian period (c. 1595–1150 BCE). The Kassite dynasty was overthrown by an invasion of another group of highlanders – the Elamites, inhabitants of southwestern Iran – and the subsequent course of events from the end of the 2nd millennium BCE until the Persian annexation of Babylonia in 539 BCE is considered by scholars to be the Neo-Babylonian period. It should be noted that the far south of Lower Mesopotamia, settled by descendants of the Akkadianized Sumerians, was often separate from the rulers in Babylon (in particular, during the so-called Dynasty of the Sealand – 1722–c. 1460 BCE).

It should be noted that the far south of Lower Mesopotamia, settled by descendants of the Akkadianized Sumerians, was often separate from the rulers in Babylon (in particular, during the so-called Dynasty of the Sealand – 1722–c. 1460 BCE).

target: Humans migrated to the lower reaches of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers relatively late, during the developed Neolithic period (6th millennium BCE). As we have already seen, the first inhabitants of southern Mesopotamia were the Subarians, who originated from the northeast, from the foothills of the Zagros Mountains. By the end of the 6th millennium BCE, they had settled the marshy region as far as the “Bitter Sea” and built the earliest known fortified settlements in Mesopotamia – proto-cities. The Subarians of Lower Mesopotamia created a distinct Ubaid archaeological culture (5th to the beginning of the 4th millennium BCE, or the “Ubaid millennium”). Soon, its Subarian bearers acquired knowledge of copper smelting (terms for which were later adopted by the Sumerians from the Ubaidians) and spread across vast territories from the Central Zagros through Upper Mesopotamia and Syria to the Mediterranean Sea, as well as in northeastern Arabia, including Bahrain. This entire vast territory, together with Lower Mesopotamia, formed a relatively homogeneous ethno-cultural area of the Subarians – the bearers of the Ubaid culture (see p. 71).

target: In the early 4th millennium BCE, a new people, the Sumerians, settled in Lower Mesopotamia. Their arrival marked the end of the Ubaid archaeological culture in this region, which was replaced by the Uruk culture. According to later Sumerian accounts, the original center of their settlement was the city of Eridu, located in the lowermost reaches of the Euphrates. The arrival of the Sumerians was largely peaceful, involving settlement within existing proto-urban centers. As previously noted, the Sumerians intermingled with the Lower Mesopotamian Ubaid population and assimilated them, adopting their craft skills, certain religious cults, and other elements of their culture.

target: The question of the Sumerians’ homeland remains unresolved. Their language has not yet been definitively linked to any known language group, although numerous candidates for such a relationship have been proposed, including the Tibeto-Burman and Polynesian languages. Despite the apparent improbability of the latter hypothesis, it is supported by linguistic evidence. From our perspective, it is most likely that the Sumerians came from the east, through Iran. According to Sumerian texts from the 3rd millennium BCE, which recount this people’s contacts with the distant central Iranian land of Aratta (in the area of modern-day Yazd), the gods of the Sumerians are venerated in Aratta, and Sumerian names are used. This may represent evidence of a Sumerian migration to Mesopotamia from the east.
